name: Karl Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or government, and your name won't go on anything you say. So you can give me the public answer and the private one. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We grow vegetables for two big supermarkets: broccoli, leeks, lettuce in summer. I start at six, drive the tractor that pulls the harvest rig, and the picking crew cut and pack on the rig as we go. Afternoons I'm in the packhouse stacking pallets or hosing down crates. It's Mr Doyle's farm, and I'm the most junior of the full-timers, so I get whatever needs doing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a field's done and it's clean and you look back at it. I don't like the supermarket rejecting a whole lorry because the broccoli heads are two centimetres too small, and then we all have to work Saturday to make it up. My partner Leila does hair in town, and between us we've got about three weeks of money put by. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's fine by me. I don't use any of that AI stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get back to work. At the farm I'd joke with the lads that the robot lettuce picker never turned up. Online, nothing, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the same as now: the supermarket still decides everything. They set the price, they set the size, and they can drop us with a phone call. AI flopping doesn't change that, so I'd still be worrying about the contract, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Maybe ask Mr Doyle for the forklift ticket so I can do more in the packhouse, because that pays a bit better. Leila and I would keep putting a bit by when we can, which honestly isn't often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When a lorry gets rejected, what happens to the vegetables?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some go to a cheaper buyer, some go to the food bank, and some get ploughed back in. It's the ploughing in that gets me. My dad grew up with nothing, and I'm driving a tractor over good food because it's the wrong size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is to blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, and everybody. The supermarket wants perfect veg because shoppers pick the perfect ones. Mr Doyle signs the contract because he needs it. I'm not one for blaming. It's just how it works, and I wish it didn't.

S0.say: I'd say good, now can we get back to work. I'd joke with the lads that the robot lettuce picker never turned up, and I wouldn't post anything online.
S0.think: The supermarket still decides everything: the price, the size, and whether we keep the contract at all. AI flopping doesn't change that, so my worry would still be the contract, not computers.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is and asks his boss for a forklift licence to get more paid packhouse work. Saves a little with his partner when money allows, which isn't often.
S0.feel: Calm, the same as any other Monday.
S0.quote: My dad grew up with nothing, and I'm driving a tractor over good food because it's the wrong size.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is plain-spoken and doesn't like to blame people, even when describing waste that clearly bothers him. His real worry is the supermarket contract, which holds all the power in his work life. He has no interest in AI tools and sees no reason to change anything in a flat picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Strong change. I've seen the videos of robot pickers. They're slow, but they're getting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it work before we panic. At the farm I'd say the robots can have the lettuce, they can't drive in the mud we had last October. I wouldn't say much else, I'm not a speech-maker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the picking crew goes first, and then the tractor driver, which is me. If the rig picks by itself, it doesn't need anyone pulling it. I'd probably last longer than the seasonal crew, because I do a bit of everything, but I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see if the robots actually work on our ground, because I'm not changing anything for a rumour. I'd get the forklift licence anyway, and maybe the lorry licence later, because the packhouse and the lorries would still need people for a while. And we'd stop going out for tea on Fridays, just to have a bit more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cough you keep telling yourself is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Mr Doyle buys one. If he does, I know. If the neighbours buy one and it sits broken in the yard, then I relax. I'm not reading the news about it, I'm watching the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use an AI tool to help you get ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila keeps saying I should ask it about the lorry licence test. I don't trust it, to be honest. I'd rather ask Mick at the depot, who's done it twice.

S1.say: I'd say let's see it work before we panic. At the farm I'd joke that the robots can have the lettuce but they can't drive in the mud we had last October.
S1.think: I think the picking crew goes first and then the tractor driver, which is me, because a rig that picks itself needs nobody to pull it. I'd last longer than the seasonal crew, but I'm not daft.
S1.do: Waits a year to see whether his boss or neighbours buy picking robots before changing anything. Gets the forklift licence and plans a lorry licence later, and cuts Friday meals out to save a little.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cough you keep telling yourself is nothing.
S1.quote: I'm not reading the news about it, I'm watching the yard.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's way of handling change is to watch what happens on his own patch, not to follow the news. He is clear-eyed that his job comes second after the picking crew, but he still waits a year before moving. He'd rather ask a person he knows than use AI, even for exam prep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... no. That's too quick for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort it out, because nobody else can. At the farm I'd say we're all in the same boat, Mr Doyle included, because if robots grow veg, the supermarkets will just buy their own farms. I'd say that to anybody, but I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in farming, and so's the lorry licence plan, because the lorries drive themselves too. I've got three weeks of money. I don't know what jobs there are when the robots can do almost anything, and I don't think anyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, Leila and I would cut back to the basics, no takeaways, no car unless we have to. I'd sign on for whatever help the government puts out. I'd ask my uncle, who has a small building firm, if there's any labouring, even though I know robots are coming for that too. Mostly I'd be waiting to see what the government does, because there's nothing I can do alone that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd probably go quiet. That's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does going quiet look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to work every day until there wasn't any. I wouldn't talk about it at home much. Leila would end up dragging it out of me at about midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two years give you time for anything at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the forklift licence, but what's the point if the forklift drives itself. With two years you don't change your life. You just hold on and hope the people in charge do something.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to sort it out, because nobody else can. I'd tell everyone at the farm we're all in the same boat, the boss included, because the supermarkets would buy their own robot farms.
S2.think: I think I'm finished in farming, and so is the lorry licence plan, because lorries will drive themselves too. I've got three weeks of money and I don't think anyone knows what jobs will be left.
S2.do: Cuts household spending to the basics straight away and signs up for any government help. Asks his uncle's building firm for labouring work, then mostly waits to see what the government does.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and likely to go quiet and keep it to himself.
S2.quote: With two years you don't change your life. You just hold on and hope the people in charge do something.
S2.fieldNote: In the fastest picture, Karl doesn't see any personal move that would work, so he puts his hope in the government. He doesn't blame anyone, even here, and sees his boss as a fellow victim of the supermarkets. His honest description of going quiet and opening up at midnight said a lot about how he copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can breathe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to make a plan, so they'd better make one. At work I'd say let's not panic yet. I'd sound calm, but I'd be keeping my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd waste the first two years. I know myself. I'd tell myself it's not here yet and keep driving the tractor. Then year three, I'd see the first robot rig on a neighbour's farm and I'd wish I'd started earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do the forklift licence in year one, because it's cheap and quick. Leila and I would try to put £80 a month aside. Around year three I'd look at whatever training the job centre offers, maybe something in repairs or maintenance, because things still break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More like a slow worry than a big fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you know you'd waste two years, what would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Doyle sitting me down and saying it straight. If the boss says it, it's real. Until then it's just telly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Leila thought about her own job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks hair is safe, because people like to chat to their hairdresser. I hope she's right. If she is, she might end up keeping us both for a bit, and I'd have to swallow my pride.

S3.say: Five years is enough for the government to make a plan, so they'd better make one. At work I'd say let's not panic yet, and I'd sound calm while keeping my eyes open.
S3.think: I'd waste the first two years telling myself it's not here yet. Then in year three I'd see the first robot rig on a neighbour's farm and wish I'd started earlier.
S3.do: Gets the forklift licence in year one and tries to save £80 a month with his partner. Around year three, looks at job centre training in repairs or maintenance.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a slow worry rather than a big fright.
S3.quote: If the boss says it, it's real. Until then it's just telly.
S3.fieldNote: Karl predicts his own delay with unusual honesty: he'd lose two of the five years waiting for proof on his doorstep. His trigger to act is his boss telling him directly. He is quietly ready to depend on his partner's income, though it would hurt his pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's still young, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone, government or the supermarkets. At the farm I'd say we've got time. I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels so far off I'd probably do nothing for five of them. That's the honest answer. Then I'd be 32, panicking, with the same three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the forklift licence and keep driving the tractor. Maybe year three or four I'd do a course in fixing machines, something with my hands, at the college on a Saturday. And Leila and I might hold off on a mortgage, because who'd lend to a farmworker when the farm's about to be robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it doesn't keep me up. That's sort of the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's sort of the problem that it doesn't keep you up. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it doesn't scare me, I won't move. I'm like that with the dentist. I go when it hurts, never before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go before it hurts, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, probably. If someone paid me to train while I still had my job, I'd do it. If I have to pay myself and lose Saturdays, I'll keep putting it off.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone, the government or the supermarkets. At the farm I'd tell people we've got time, and I'd mean it.
S4.think: Ten years feels so far off I'd probably do nothing for five of them. Then I'd be 32, panicking, with the same three weeks of money.
S4.do: Gets the forklift licence in year one and keeps driving the tractor. Around year three or four takes a Saturday college course in machine repair, and delays plans for a mortgage with his partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not losing sleep, which he sees as the problem.
S4.quote: If it doesn't scare me, I won't move. I'm like that with the dentist. I go when it hurts, never before.
S4.fieldNote: More time doesn't make Karl more active; it makes him more likely to put things off, and he says so plainly. His answer about what would help is precise: paid training while still employed. That suggests outside support matters more for him than warning time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. There's no time to do anything, and I'm not a fast mover. What would help is the government paying people like me to train while we still have the job, and a bit of money each month if the job goes, so Leila doesn't have to carry both of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the food. If robots grow it all, will it still be thrown away for being the wrong size? I'd like to know someone's thought about that.

headlineQuote: If it doesn't scare me, I won't move. I'm like that with the dentist. I go when it hurts, never before.
portrait: Karl Ibrahim is a 27-year-old junior worker on a vegetable farm that supplies supermarkets, where he drives the harvest rig tractor and stacks pallets in the packhouse. He lives with his partner Leila, a hairdresser, and they have about three weeks of savings. He never uses AI, avoids blaming anyone and sees the supermarket contract as the real power in his life. Across all the pictures he waits for proof on his own doorstep, and he admits that more warning time only makes him put things off for longer. In AGI by 2028 he expects to hold on and hope the government acts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to act and he knows he's not a fast mover.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training while people still have their jobs, and a monthly payment if the job goes so his partner doesn't have to carry them both.
